related_questions.question: Can pneumonia cause interstitial lung disease?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, pneumonia can, in some cases, lead to interstitial lung disease (ILD), specifically a type called interstitial pneumonia. While pneumonia primarily affects the air sacs (alveoli) of the lungs, it can also cause inflammation and damage to the interstitium, the tissue surrounding the air sacs, leading to ILD.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, pneumonia can, in some cases, lead to interstitial lung disease (ILD)

list.title: Pneumonia and Interstitial Lung Disease:
list.snippet: Pneumonia is an infection that inflames the air sacs in one or both lungs. This inflammation can sometimes extend into the interstitium, the supporting framework of the lungs.

list.title: Interstitial Pneumonia:
list.snippet: When the inflammation primarily affects the interstitium, it is referred to as interstitial pneumonia.

list.title: Causes of Interstitial Pneumonia:
list.snippet: Interstitial pneumonia can be caused by various factors, including bacteria, viruses, or fungi. For example, Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a common bacterial cause of interstitial pneumonia.

list.title: ILD as a Complication:
list.snippet: In some cases, severe pneumonia can lead to lung scarring (pulmonary fibrosis), which is a characteristic feature of some types of ILD.

list.title: Other ILDs:
list.snippet: While interstitial pneumonia is a specific type of ILD, other forms of ILD can also develop, sometimes linked to autoimmune conditions or environmental factors, but not directly caused by pneumonia.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, pneumonia, particularly severe cases, can cause interstitial pneumonia, a specific form of ILD. While pneumonia is not the sole cause of all ILDs, it can contribute to the development of this lung condition in some instances.

related_questions.question: What disorders are associated with interstitial lung disease?
related_questions.snippet: Known causes of interstitial lung disease include: Connective tissue disease, including rheumatoid arthritis (RA), lupus and scleroderma. Granulomatous disease, like sarcoidosis. Inhaling certain substances, like asbestos, silica, tobacco and beryllium.
